meta.title: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce delivery in 2027?
meta.subtitle: Discussion document for the board, January 2027
meta.purpose: Should Parcelbird launch Parcelbird Now, its own 15-minute grocery delivery in Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City, in 2027, while keeping 12 months of runway on its $12.0M of cash?
meta.confidentiality: Board confidential. Synthetic benchmark data: company and figures are fictional

inputs.label: Parcelbird board briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data)
Modelling assumptions chosen on the board's behalf (user unavailable at the storyline review)
inputs.content: Stores trade 365 days a year; rider pay sensitivity uses a $1-an-hour step; software stress cases use 40% and 30% ARR growth a year in 2027 and 2028.

storyline.governing_thought: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027: its stores would lose money on every order and break the runway rule; grow the software business instead

exec_summary.text: Quick commerce is booming, but its operators lose money on every order

sub_points.text: US sales nearly tripled from 2022 to 2025, yet Zipcart lost $1.90 and QuickBasket $3.40 an order

exec_summary.text: A Parcelbird store would lose about $6 an order at the benchmark of 14 sites

sub_points.text: The plan's profit rests on order value and rider productivity above any site
Only 22% of pop-up customers still ordered in month three

exec_summary.text: The launch breaks the cash rule: Parcelbird would be at least $1.9M short at month 18

sub_points.text: Nine stores at benchmark economics would lose about $18M a year
A one-store pilot would cost about $2.6M to confirm a loss

exec_summary.text: The software business can reach breakeven in early 2029 within today's cash

sub_points.text: Cash bottoms out at about $5.4M at end-2028; the runway rule holds at 40% growth, not at 30%

exec_summary.text: Approve software first and sell grocers store-based fast delivery

sub_points.text: Four gates, led by ARR growth of at least 40%, from mid-2027
Reopen own delivery only if a customer site makes money after its fixed costs

next_steps.action: Decide not to launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; close the pop-up and keep its data
Approve two engineers and two sales hires for the software business
Scope store-based fast delivery with the pipeline grocers that asked for it
Report the four gates monthly: signed ARR, growth, cash against burn, site productivity
Hold the mid-year gate review and set the 2028 reopen check

constraints.item: Keep at least 12 months of runway at all times
constraints.effect: the launch breaks it at month 18 on every reading; the software plan is tested against it at each year-end

constraints.item: No new funding round for a delivery operator
constraints.effect: the cash gap cannot be refinanced, so the launch is tested against today's $12.0M only

constraints.item: Software burn continues during the launch
constraints.effect: adds $4.4M over 18 months on the same falling-burn basis as the software case ($7.2M at today's flat rate)

constraints.item: Two engineers and two sales hires, about $0.8M a year
constraints.effect: included in the software cost base, raising breakeven ARR to $11.0M

constraints.item: Possible minimum pay standards for riders in two of three cities
constraints.effect: every $1 an hour adds about $0.42 an order; it can only worsen the launch case

constraints.item: Promotions the pop-up needed to grow (12% of order value)
constraints.effect: the plan's 2% is shown against it

alternatives.option: A one-store Columbus pilot instead of nine stores
alternatives.why: costs about $2.6M, breaks the runway rule at 40% software growth, and at the median can only confirm a loss

alternatives.option: Launch with a Zipcart-style $3.99 fee and 1% promotions
alternatives.why: makes the order positive but the store profits only at the best site's density; kept as a reopen condition

alternatives.option: Run the temporary pop-up six more months as a cheap density test
alternatives.why: about $0.6M of losses, but at 280 orders a day it cannot reach the density at which the answer would change; customer sites show that for free

alternatives.option: Software first, plus store-based fast delivery sold to grocers
alternatives.why: reaches breakeven within the cash, keeps the runway rule at 40% growth and keeps grocers as customers

failure_threshold.driver: software ARR growth a year in 2027–28
failure_threshold.threshold: the runway rule breaks in 2028 if growth falls to 30%; it holds at 40%

consistency.headline: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027: its stores would lose money on every order and break the runway rule; grow the software business instead

cases.base: software plan at 60% growth: breakeven in early 2029, cash low point about $5.4M at end-2028
cases.stress: at 40% growth cash ends 2028 at $3.7M, $1.3M above the runway need ($0.4M on trailing burn, $0.5M if January cash is two months lower); the launch fails in both cases

gates.threshold: under $1.23M by end of June 2027 (half a 60% year)
gates.response: defer the two sales hires and cut burn
cut costs before the runway rule breaks (it does at 30%)

gates.metric: a customer site's profit per order after its fixed costs
gates.threshold: profit per order above $0 after the site's fixed costs, two quarters in a row
gates.response: reopen own delivery with a costed one-store plan

problem.statement: Should Parcelbird launch Parcelbird Now, its own 15-minute grocery delivery in Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City, in 2027, while keeping 12 months of runway on its $12.0M of cash?
problem.decision_maker: Board of Parcelbird (two founders, two investors): approve or reject the launch
success_criteria: Positive profit per order on evidence Parcelbird has, not only on plan inputs
Funded within today's $12.0M of cash, with no new round
At least 12 months of runway at all times
A path to company profitability within the current cash
problem.accuracy: Directional: enough to say yes or no, with the thresholds that would change the answer
out_of_scope: Cities beyond Columbus, Indianapolis and Kansas City

one_day_answer.situation: Parcelbird's software runs dark stores for grocers, with $4.1M of ARR growing 60% a year and $12.0M in cash
one_day_answer.complication: The founders want to become an operator in a market growing over 40% a year, but its operators lose money per order and the plan needs most of the cash
one_day_answer.resolution: Do not launch in 2027; fund the software business to breakeven, sell grocers fast delivery from their own stores, and reopen the question only if a site proves the economics
